decision: DIFFERS -> W1: author the page's figure. uga_ext C1005 Home Garden Peppers (names 'Sweet Banana' among its cultivars; same species C. annuum) states "When planting, space pepper plants 12–24 in. apart in the row, with rows about 3 ft apart." -> in_row [12,24], row [36,36]. Today's [12,18] is a two-page blend (Clemson 12 lo + UMN/ISU 18 hi) that no cited page states; VCE 426-331 Table 5 ('Peppers 12-24 in 30-36 in') and UMD ('12"- 24" in-rows x 30"- 36"') agree with UGA on 12-24. The four prose restatements of 12-18 are re-authored to 12-24 in the same promote (R3).

edits.new: Harden the plants off over about a week, then plant them 12 to 24 inches apart into warm soil. A sheet of black plastic mulch warms the soil, and mulch of any kind helps keep watering even.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (UGA C1005: 12-24 in)

edits.new: Harden off over 7 to 10 days, then transplant into warm soil, 12 to 24 inches apart in rows about 3 feet apart. Black plastic or fabric mulch warms the soil and gives a warm-season crop a head start; mulch also steadies moisture against blossom-end rot.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (UGA C1005: 12-24 in)

edits.new: Start banana pepper seeds indoors about 8 weeks before you plan to plant out, keeping them warm (80 to 90°F) to sprout well. Peppers need more warmth and a longer head start than many crops, and they go outside only once the soil is warm (about 60 to 65°F) and nights stay above 50 to 55°F. Use stocky transplants and space them 12 to 24 inches apart.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (UGA C1005: 12-24 in)

edits.new: Start banana pepper seeds indoors about 8 weeks before transplanting (Georgia and Clemson use 6 to 8 weeks; Maryland 8 to 10), with bottom heat of 80 to 90°F for fast, even germination. Peppers need warmth and a longer indoor head start than many vegetables and are set out after the soil has warmed to 60 to 65°F and nights hold above 50 to 55°F. Choose sturdy transplants and set them 12 to 24 inches apart in rows about 3 feet apart. Direct sowing is practical only in the longest, warmest regions; nearly everywhere this is a transplant crop.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (UGA C1005: 12-24 in)
